title: Stories That Travel
bigQuestion: How do people keep a faith alive by telling it, and how do faiths travel with people to new places?

story.title: Remember It, Don't Write It
story.kicker: A visiting elder shares a story and asks the class to hold it in their memory.
paragraphs: Snow covers the playground. Inside Room 12, the class sits in a circle on the rug. A guest has come to visit. She is an Anishinaabe elder, which means a respected older person in her Native nation.
Before she starts, she smiles. "Please put your pencils down," she says. "Today I want you to remember with your ears and your heart, not your paper. That is how my grandmother taught me."

She tells a story of a time long ago when water covered the world. The animals tried to dive down and bring up a little mud. Many could not reach the bottom. At last the small muskrat came up with mud in its paw.

The mud was placed on a turtle's back, and it grew into land. "That is why many of our people call this land Turtle Island," she says. "Our stories also tell how the lakes and the land are gifts to care for."

When she finishes, the room is quiet. "Now you carry a piece of this story," she says. "Tell it gently. And remember that some of our stories are only for our own people. I shared this one because it is okay to share."
story.think: Why do you think the elder asked the class to remember the story instead of writing it down?

lessons.title: What Is an Oral Tradition?
lessons.mainIdea: An oral tradition is knowledge passed down by speaking, singing and remembering, not only by writing.
reading: Some faiths have one main holy book. Christians read the Bible. Muslims read the Qur'an. But many faiths around the world have been kept mainly by telling, from older people to younger people.

This is called an *oral tradition*. Oral means spoken. Stories, songs, prayers and teachings are learned by listening and remembering. They are passed on at family gatherings, ceremonies and quiet evenings.
Even faiths with holy books use telling. The Torah tells parents to teach its words to their children at home and on the road. Many Jewish families still say prayers from memory each day.

words.d: stories, songs and teachings passed down by speaking and remembering
a respected older person who carries the knowledge of a community

look.title: Teach Them at Home
look.text: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
look.prompt: List the times this verse says to talk about its teachings. What does this show about spoken teaching?

check.q: What does oral mean?
check.why: Oral means spoken. An oral tradition is passed down by speaking and remembering.

check.q: Who often carries oral traditions in a community?
check.why: Elders are respected older people who pass on stories and teachings to younger people.

check.q: According to Deuteronomy 6:7, where should parents talk about its teachings?
choices: At home and on the road
check.why: The verse says to talk of them when you sit in your house and walk by the way.

lessons.title: Memory and Respect
lessons.mainIdea: In oral traditions, people remember stories carefully and tell them with respect.
reading: How can a story last hundreds of years with no book? People listen many times. They hear it at the same season each year. They learn the words, the pauses and even the way to sit while listening.
Tellers often use *repetition*, saying key parts again and again. Songs, drumming and rhythm help too. It is much easier to remember words that you sing than words you only read once.
In many Native communities, a story is more than fun. Adherents see it as a teaching about how to live. Listening quietly and remembering well are ways of showing respect to the teller and the story.

words.d: saying or doing something again and again
a special set of actions done in a set way for an important reason

look.title: Try to Remember
look.text: Your teacher says a short story once. Then she sings it to a drumbeat three times. The next day, you try to say it back.
look.prompt: Which way do you think helps you remember better, hearing it once or singing it three times? Why?

check.q: What is repetition?
check.why: Repetition means saying or doing something again and again, which helps memory.

check.q: Which helps people remember oral stories?
check.why: Songs, rhythm and repetition help listeners remember stories well.

check.q: In many Native communities, how is a story seen?
choices: As a teaching about how to live
check.why: Many Native adherents see stories as teachings about how to live, not just entertainment.

lessons.title: Stories With Permission
lessons.mainIdea: Some stories are shared with everyone, and some are only for members of a community or for certain times.
reading: Not every story is meant for everyone. In many Native nations, some stories are sacred and kept within the community. Outsiders are asked not to retell them or write them down.
Some stories also have a right time. In many Anishinaabe families, certain sacred stories are told only in winter, when snow is on the ground. Other stories may be shared at any time.
So a respectful learner asks *permission*. You might ask, "Is this a story I may share?" If the answer is no, you honor it. Learning about a faith includes respecting what its people choose to keep.

words.d: being told yes, it is okay to do something
holy or deeply special to a faith; treated with great care

look.title: What Would You Do?
look.text: A friend from a Native nation tells you part of a family story. Later, she says it is a sacred story her family keeps private. You were planning to use it in your class poster.
look.prompt: What should you do? What question could you ask before sharing someone's story in the future?

check.q: What does sacred mean?
choices: Holy or deeply special to a faith
check.why: Sacred means holy or deeply special, treated with great care.

check.q: When are certain Anishinaabe sacred stories often told?
choices: In winter, when snow is on the ground
check.why: In many Anishinaabe families, certain sacred stories are told only in winter.

check.q: What should a respectful learner do before retelling someone's story?
check.why: Some stories are private, so a respectful learner asks permission first.

lessons.title: People of the Great Lakes
lessons.mainIdea: The Potawatomi, Ojibwe and Odawa have lived around the Great Lakes for a very long time and still live here today.
reading: Long before Chicago was a city, Native nations lived around the Great Lakes. Three nations, the Potawatomi, Ojibwe and Odawa, call themselves Anishinaabe. They are often called the *Council of Three Fires*.
The name Chicago likely comes from a Native word for a wild onion that grew along the river. Native people fished, farmed, gathered wild rice and traveled the lakes by canoe.
Native nations are not only in the past. Today Chicago has one of the largest urban Native American communities in the country. Many families keep their languages, stories and ceremonies alive.

words.d: a name the Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi peoples use for themselves
the long alliance of the Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi nations

look.title: Then and Now
look.text: Picture Lake Michigan long ago. Canoes glide by the shore. Now picture the same lake today. A Native family gathers at a powwow in a Chicago park, with drums and dancing.
look.prompt: What is the same in both pictures? Why is it important to know Native nations are still here?

check.q: Which three nations make up the Council of Three Fires?
check.why: The Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi form the Council of Three Fires.

check.q: Where does the name Chicago likely come from?
choices: A Native word for a wild onion
check.why: The name Chicago likely comes from a Native word for a wild onion along the river.

check.q: Which statement about Native nations is true?
choices: They are only in the past
Many Native families live in Chicago today
check.why: Chicago has a large Native community today that keeps languages and stories alive.

lessons.title: Turtle Island
lessons.mainIdea: Many Anishinaabe people tell a creation story in which the land was formed on a turtle's back.
reading: A *creation story* tells how the world or a people began. Many faiths have one. The Bible's book of Genesis opens with God creating the heaven and the earth over six days.
Many Anishinaabe tell of a great flood. A hero named Nanabozho and the animals needed land. The muskrat dove deep and brought up mud. The mud was placed on a turtle's back, and it grew into land.

That is why many Native people call North America Turtle Island. For adherents, the story teaches that small creatures matter and that the land is a gift. The same story has different versions in different families.

words.d: a story that tells how the world or a people began
a name many Native people use for North America, from their creation stories

look.title: Another Beginning
look.text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
look.prompt: Compare this line with the Turtle Island story. How does each story say the land began?

check.q: In the Anishinaabe story, which animal brought up the mud?
check.why: In many versions, the small muskrat dove deep and brought up mud for the land.

check.q: What does Turtle Island mean for many Native people?
choices: A small island in a lake
check.why: Many Native people call North America Turtle Island, from their creation stories.

check.q: Which book opens with the line about God creating the heaven and the earth?
check.why: Genesis, the first book of the Bible, opens with that line.

lessons.title: The Yoruba and the Orishas
lessons.mainIdea: The Yoruba of West Africa pass on teachings about God, the orishas and the ancestors mostly by telling and ceremony.
reading: The Yoruba people live mainly in Nigeria and nearby countries in West Africa. Their faith has been kept for centuries through stories, songs, drumming and ceremonies, not one single book.

Many Yoruba believe in one high God, Olodumare. They also honor the *orishas*, powerful spirits linked to parts of nature and life. One story tells how the orisha Obatala came down and spread earth over the waters to make land.

*Ancestors* matter too. Adherents believe family members who have died still watch over the living. Families remember them with prayers, food and festivals. Priests memorize many sacred verses called Ifá.

words.d: in Yoruba religion, a powerful spirit linked to parts of nature and life
a family member who lived long ago
in Yoruba belief, the one high God

look.title: Two Stories of Land
look.text: Story A (Anishinaabe): A muskrat brings mud from under the water. It is placed on a turtle's back and grows into land. Story B (Yoruba): The orisha Obatala comes down and spreads earth over the waters to make land.
look.prompt: What is alike in these two stories? What is different?

check.q: Where do most Yoruba people live?
check.why: The Yoruba live mainly in Nigeria and nearby countries in West Africa.

check.q: What are the orishas?
check.why: In Yoruba religion, orishas are powerful spirits linked to nature and life.

check.q: How do many Yoruba families honor ancestors?
check.why: Many Yoruba remember ancestors with prayers, food and festivals.

lessons.title: Across the Ocean
lessons.mainIdea: When people move, they carry their faith with them, and it can grow in new places.
reading: Faiths travel with people. When Yoruba people were taken to the Americas as enslaved people, many kept their beliefs alive in secret. Their faith helped form new traditions in Cuba and Brazil.

In Cuba, one tradition is called Santería or Lucumí. In Brazil, one is called Candomblé. Followers honor the orishas with drumming, songs and dance. Today these traditions have followers in Chicago too.
This shows how faiths *adapt*. They keep old teachings and take on new forms in new places. Moving can bring hard times, and faith often helps people stay connected to home.

words.d: to change to fit a new place or situation
forced to work for others without freedom or pay

look.title: Carry It With You
look.text: Imagine your family must move far away. You can only bring what you carry in your memory: songs, prayers, stories and holiday customs.
look.prompt: Which things would you most want to remember? How might they change in a new home?

check.q: Which tradition grew from Yoruba roots in Cuba?
check.why: Santería, also called Lucumí, grew in Cuba from Yoruba roots.

check.q: What does adapt mean?
choices: To change to fit a new place
check.why: To adapt is to change to fit a new place or situation.

check.q: Where did Candomblé grow?
check.why: Candomblé is a tradition with Yoruba roots that grew in Brazil.

lessons.title: The Great Migration
lessons.mainIdea: In the Great Migration, millions of Black Americans moved north, and their churches helped build Chicago.
reading: From about 1916 to 1970, around six million Black Americans left the South. They moved to northern and western cities to find jobs and escape unfair laws. This was the *Great Migration*.
Hundreds of thousands came to Chicago. They brought their faith, mostly Baptist and Methodist Christianity. They filled old churches and started many new ones on the South Side.

Chicago churches became famous for *gospel music*. Thomas A. Dorsey, often called the father of gospel music, led a choir at Pilgrim Baptist Church. Singer Mahalia Jackson made Chicago gospel known around the world.

words.d: the move of millions of Black Americans from the South to northern and western cities, c. 1916 to 1970
Christian music with strong singing, born in Black churches

look.title: The Great Migration in Numbers
look.cite: Common historical estimates, e.g. U.S. Census Bureau and the Library of Congress
look.prompt: About how many years did the Great Migration last? Why might churches matter to people starting over?

check.q: What was the Great Migration?
choices: Black Americans moving from the South to northern cities
check.why: In the Great Migration, millions of Black Americans left the South for northern and western cities.

check.q: Who is often called the father of gospel music?
check.why: Thomas A. Dorsey led a choir at Pilgrim Baptist Church in Chicago and is often called the father of gospel music.

check.q: Which faith did most Great Migration families bring to Chicago?
check.why: Most families brought Baptist and Methodist Christianity and built many churches on the South Side.

lessons.title: New Neighbors, New Temples
lessons.mainIdea: Immigrants from around the world brought churches, synagogues, temples, mosques and gurdwaras to the Chicago area.
reading: Chicago has always been a city of *immigrants*. In the 1800s and early 1900s, people came from Ireland, Germany, Poland, Italy and Eastern Europe. They built Catholic and Protestant churches and Jewish synagogues.
Later, many families came from Mexico and Latin America, bringing Catholic parishes full of Spanish-language masses. After 1965, new U.S. laws let more people come from Asia and Africa.
Those newcomers built Hindu and Buddhist temples, mosques and Sikh gurdwaras across the Chicago area. Walk down Devon Avenue on the North Side and you can see many cultures and faiths on one street.

words.d: a person who moves to a new country to live
a local church community, often Catholic, and the area it serves

look.title: Waves of Newcomers
look.cite: Common historical dates for Chicago immigration; Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965
look.prompt: Put these moves in order. Which change opened the door to more temples and mosques?

check.q: What is an immigrant?
choices: A person who moves to a new country to live
A kind of house of worship
check.why: An immigrant is a person who moves to a new country to live.

check.q: What happened after new U.S. laws in 1965?
choices: More people could come from Asia and Africa
check.why: The 1965 law let more people come from Asia and Africa, who built temples, mosques and gurdwaras.

check.q: What might you see on Devon Avenue?
choices: Many cultures and faiths on one street
check.why: Devon Avenue on the North Side is known for many cultures and faiths side by side.

choices: Knowledge passed down by speaking and remembering
review.why: An oral tradition is passed down by speaking, singing and remembering.

review.q: In the story, why did the elder ask students to put down pencils?
choices: To remember with ears and heart, as she was taught
Because writing is against the law
review.why: She wanted them to learn the way her grandmother taught her, by listening and remembering.

review.q: What should you do if a story is sacred and kept private?
choices: Change a few words and share it
Honor the choice and not retell it
review.why: A respectful learner asks permission and honors a community's choice to keep some stories private.

choices: Olodumare: the high God in Yoruba belief
review.why: In Yoruba belief, Olodumare is the one high God.

review.q: How are the Anishinaabe and Yoruba creation stories alike?
choices: Both begin with land made from the waters
Both are from the same book
Both are about a flood of fire
review.why: In both stories, land is made where there was only water.

review.q: Which of these came to Chicago during the Great Migration?
review.why: Black families from the South brought and built Baptist and Methodist churches in Chicago.

review.q: Which word means to change to fit a new place?
review.why: To adapt is to change to fit a new place, as faiths do when people move.

review.q: Which nations form the Council of Three Fires?
review.why: The Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi form the Council of Three Fires.
